screens.title: Ethereum: The Foundation for Smart Contracts and dApps
screens.narratorSegment: Ethereum extended the idea of a blockchain into a programmable platform, allowing developers to embed logic that runs across a distributed network. In practice, that means instead of just recording transfers of value, Ethereum hosts self-executing programs called smart contracts that run deterministically on a runtime called the EVM, or Ethereum Virtual Machine. This capability turned blockchains into a substrate for decentralized applications, powering everything from decentralized finance to digital collectibles. As you begin building with Web3. js, you'll use this foundation to deploy contracts, call functions, and handle the real costs and constraints of on-chain computation. A few practical distinctions matter early: Ether is used to pay for computational work called gas; accounts come in two forms—EOAs you control with a private key, and contract accounts governed by deployed code; and the EVM ensures every node reaches the same result when code runs. Keep these ideas in mind as the conceptual scaffolding for our hands-on Web3 work. How will these pieces influence the design and cost of your dApp?

Module 2 › Chapter 1.4 › Overview
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass

Ethereum: The Foundation for Smart Contracts and dApps

This lesson explains how Ethereum evolved a blockchain into a platform for code, why the EVM matters for determinism, how smart contracts automate agreements, and why gas and account types shape every transaction you build with Web3.js.

Concept Map
EVM
Deterministic runtime executing bytecode
Smart Contracts
Immutable code that enforces rules
Gas
Fuel for computation paid in ETH
Explore Key Topics
EVM & Determinism
Runtime ensuring the same result on every node; compiled smart contract bytecode runs here.
Smart Contracts
Self-executing code deployed as contracts; immutable and addressable on-chain.
Gas & Accounts
Gas measures computation; EOAs and Contract Accounts behave differently for signing and execution.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: By the end of this chapter you should be able to explain why Ethereum is different from a simple ledger, describe how the EVM executes code deterministically, and define what smart contracts do in a dApp. You will also learn to explain gas as a unit of computational work and recognize how gas price and gas limit influence transaction cost and success. Practically, you'll know the difference between an externally owned account and a contract account, how wallets like MetaMask act as EOAs, and why deployed contracts lack private keys. These competencies matter because they guide how you design interactions with a contract and how you estimate cost and security. For example, choosing to do heavy computation on-chain increases gas cost and should influence how you structure your contract versus off-chain logic. Each objective lists a concrete skill and a verification milestone so you can confirm readiness before coding with Web3. js.

screens.title: Bitcoin vs Ethereum — Purpose and Programmability
screens.narratorSegment: At a high level, Bitcoin and Ethereum both provide decentralized ledgers, but they were designed with different primary purposes. Bitcoin focuses on secure, peer-to-peer transfer of value and serves as a digital store of value. By contrast, Ethereum was created to be programmable: it runs arbitrary code in the form of smart contracts. That difference matters when you decide which platform fits an application. For example, if your project only needs secure payments, a simple ledger is sufficient; but if you require automated, enforceable logic—like an escrow that releases funds when documented conditions are met—Ethereum's programmability provides the tooling. Another important distinction is operational: Ethereum maintains an execution environment, the EVM, which processes contract bytecode deterministically across nodes; Bitcoin's script is intentionally limited and not Turing-complete. A common misconception is to assume all blockchains are interchangeable; they are not. Design decisions—immutability, gas costs, execution model—affect security, performance, and cost for developers. Consider these trade-offs early, because they influence how you architect your dApp and whether logic belongs on-chain or off-chain. What part of your application truly requires global consensus? Bitcoin vs Ethereum — Purpose and Programmability means bitcoin is a ledger for value transfer; ethereum is a programmable platform for code that runs on-chain.. In practical terms, how ethereum's goals differ from bitcoin's original design. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Comparison insight
keyIdea.text: Bitcoin is a ledger for value transfer; Ethereum is a programmable platform for code that runs on-chain.

content.html:
Comparison

Bitcoin: Ledger-first

Designed primarily for secure peer-to-peer transfers and store of value. Scripting is limited and focused on transaction validation.

Primary use
Value transfer and censorship-resistant money.
Execution model
Limited script for validation, not a general runtime.
When to choose
Simple payments and store-of-value applications.
Why it matters

Choosing a platform affects what logic can run on-chain and how much it costs. Programmability comes with complexity and gas costs.

Comparison

Ethereum: Programmable platform

Runs deterministic smart contract bytecode on the EVM so developers can build dApps with on-chain logic and state.

Primary use
Deployable programs and decentralized applications.
Execution model
EVM executes bytecode deterministically across nodes.
When to choose
Applications requiring enforced on-chain rules, transparency, and composability.
Key takeaway

Use Ethereum when your application needs on-chain enforcement or interoperable on-chain state; otherwise prefer simpler ledgers.

screens.title: What is the Ethereum Virtual Machine (EVM)?
screens.narratorSegment: The Ethereum Virtual Machine is the environment where smart contract code runs. Think of the EVM as a sandboxed C P U that every full node runs; it takes the contract's bytecode, executes instructions, and alters the global state in a way that every node can reproduce. Deterministic execution is critical: the same inputs must always produce the same outputs across validators so that consensus on the ledger's state is possible. Developers usually write contracts in a high-level language, such as Solidity, which a compiler converts into EVM bytecode. When a contract function is called, nodes simulate the bytecode execution with the same gas accounting so that the cost and effects are consistent. A concrete example: if a contract's function deducts tokens and emits an event, the EVM applies those state changes identically on every node. A common misconception is that the EVM executes code faster because it runs everywhere; in reality, it enforces determinism and isolation, and complex on-chain computation means higher gas costs. The practical takeaway is to design contracts with predictable, efficient logic because the EVM will execute every instruction you deploy.

keyIdea.title: EVM in one line
keyIdea.text: A deterministic, isolated runtime that executes smart contract bytecode and produces identical state changes across nodes.

content.html:
Definition

Ethereum Virtual Machine (EVM)

A sandboxed runtime ensuring deterministic execution of smart contract bytecode on every node.

Role
Execute bytecode, update state, and enforce gas accounting consistently.
Input
Contract bytecode and transaction data.
Output
Deterministic state changes and logs visible on-chain.
Analogy

Sandboxed CPU for blockchain programs

Like a CPU that runs a program and changes memory, the EVM runs bytecode and updates the blockchain state. Because every node runs the same program, consensus is preserved.

Concrete example
A token transfer function reduces the sender balance and increases the receiver balance; the EVM enforces both changes identically on all nodes.
Common misconception
The EVM is not a fast distributed computer; it's a deterministic runtime where every instruction costs gas and must be chosen carefully.
Key takeaway

Design efficient, deterministic contract logic because the EVM executes every step and charges gas for it.

screens.title: Smart Contracts — Self-executing agreements as code
screens.narratorSegment: Smart contracts are programs deployed to the Ethereum blockchain that execute automatically when called and when predefined conditions are met. They encapsulate rules and state; once deployed, their bytecode and storage are stored on-chain and cannot be altered, which enforces immutability and transparency. An everyday example is an escrow-like contract that releases payment when a milestone is confirmed: the contract holds funds and, after receiving an interaction that satisfies the escrow condition, executes the transfer. Because contracts are immutable after deployment, testing and design matter; mistakes in logic become permanent and often costly. A common misconception is that smart contracts eliminate trust entirely; in reality, they replace certain human intermediaries with code, but trust shifts to the contract's correctness and the security of its implementation. When building dApps, you combine front-end interfaces with contract functions to create user experiences; the contract becomes the authoritative backend. The important practical insight is to keep on-chain logic lean, minimize attack surface, and plan upgradeability or migration patterns if you expect future changes. Smart Contracts — Self-executing agreements as code means smart contracts are immutable code on-chain that enforce rules and change state when their conditions are met.. In practical terms, how contracts encode rules, enforce actions, and become dapp backends. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Smart contract core
keyIdea.text: Smart contracts are immutable code on-chain that enforce rules and change state when their conditions are met.

content.html:
Definition

Smart Contract

A deployed program that executes when called and enforces on-chain rules and state changes.

Properties
Immutable bytecode, on-chain storage, addressable, and callable by transactions.
Example
An escrow contract that releases funds when a deliverable is confirmed.
Risk
Bugs are permanent; thorough testing and audits reduce the chance of costly errors.
Analogy & Practice

Smart contracts as dApp backends

A front-end interacts with a contract via transactions or calls, and the contract enforces the rules reliably on-chain.

Concrete scenario
A marketplace contract that transfers NFT ownership and emits events for indexing when a sale completes.
Misconception
Contracts do not guarantee correctness beyond their code. They automate rules, but the rules must be correct and secure.
Key takeaway

Treat contracts as immutable backends: plan carefully, write tests, and keep heavy computation off-chain when possible.

screens.title: Smart Contract Lifecycle: Compile, Deploy, Interact
screens.narratorSegment: A smart contract moves through a clear lifecycle: you write high-level code, compile it to EVM bytecode, deploy that bytecode in a transaction, and then interact with the deployed contract by sending transactions or calls. First, writing in a high-level language like Solidity makes contracts readable and easier to test. Compilation translates functions and data structures into bytecode the EVM understands. Deployment is a transaction that stores this bytecode at a contract address; deployment consumes gas because it writes data to the chain. Once deployed, interacting with the contract also consumes gas for state-changing operations, while read-only calls can often be executed off-chain without gas if they don't change state. A concrete example: you write a token contract, compile it, deploy to a testnet, and then call its transfer function to move tokens; every state change will be recorded on-chain and costs gas. Common mistakes include forgetting to set a sufficient gas limit for deployment and neglecting to test migrations across networks. The practical advice is to test on a testnet, verify gas estimates before broad deployment, and keep deployable bytecode size and complexity in mind to control cost.

keyIdea.title: Lifecycle summary
keyIdea.text: Code → compile → deploy (costly) → interact; each step has gas and testing implications that affect cost and safety.

content.html:
Process Flow

Compile → Deploy → Interact

A step-by-step progression from human-readable code to on-chain execution; each step affects cost and behavior.

1
Write & Test
Author contracts in Solidity and run unit tests locally to catch logic errors before deployment.
2
Compile
Compiler turns code into EVM bytecode and ABI; both are needed for deployment and interaction.
3
Deploy
A deployment transaction writes bytecode to-chain and assigns an address; this is gas-costly and immutable.
4
Interact
Send transactions for state changes or call view functions for reads; transactions consume gas and require signing by an EOA.
Concrete example
Deploy a token contract to a testnet then call transfer; the deploy and transfer both consume gas but the read balance call does not if executed off-chain.
Common mistake
Underestimating gas for deployment or testing only on mainnet without testnet runs leads to high cost and errors.
Key takeaway

Use testnets to validate logic and estimate gas before mainnet deployment to avoid permanent mistakes.

screens.title: Gas: Fuel for Ethereum Transactions
screens.narratorSegment: Gas is how Ethereum measures the computational effort required to run operations on-chain. Every opcode executed by the EVM has an associated gas cost; simple transfers use little gas, while complex contract functions use more. Two values matter for every transaction: the gas limit, which caps the maximum gas you're willing to spend, and the gas price, which is the amount of Ether you pay per unit of gas. The product of gas limit and gas price is the maximum you might pay, though you only pay for the gas actually used. Choosing a low gas price during network congestion can delay your transaction or cause it to be ignored, while a too-low gas limit will run out of gas and revert state changes while still consuming the spent gas. A common beginner error is to underestimate gas for contract deployment or complex interactions; this results in failed transactions and lost gas. As a concrete example, deploying a contract that stores a lot of data requires a high gas limit and will be expensive. When using Web3. js you will commonly estimate gas programmatically before sending transactions, but you must still interpret those estimates and choose appropriate price settings. The key practical skill is to reason about cost versus on-chain necessity and to use testnets for realistic estimation.

keyIdea.title: Gas principle
keyIdea.text: Gas measures computation; gas limit caps execution, gas price sets priority, and their product bounds transaction cost.

content.html:
Definition

Gas, Gas Limit, Gas Price

Gas quantifies computation; gas limit prevents runaway execution and gas price signals how quickly you want miners/validators to include the transaction.

Gas unit
Cost per opcode executed.
Gas limit
Maximum gas allowed for the transaction.
Gas price
ETH paid per gas unit; determines priority.
Concrete example
If a deployment consumes 3,000,000 gas and you set a price, the cost equals gas used times gas price; set a safe gas limit above expected use to avoid revert.
Practical notes
Use Web3.js gas estimation helpers, check network congestion, and test on a testnet to get realistic numbers before spending real ETH.
Common mistake
Underestimating gas limit causes reverts; failing to adjust gas price during congestion causes long delays.
Key takeaway

Treat gas as a deliberate budget: estimate, test, and set limits and prices to balance cost and speed.

screens.title: EOA vs Contract Account
screens.narratorSegment: Ethereum has two primary account types that behave differently: Externally Owned Accounts and Contract Accounts. An EOA is controlled by a private key; it has an address and can initiate transactions by signing them. Wallets like MetaMask represent EOAs. A Contract Account, however, is controlled by code: it has bytecode stored at its address and executes that code when it receives a call. Contract accounts cannot sign transactions because they do not have private keys; they execute in response to transactions initiated by EOAs or other contracts. A useful concrete contrast: to transfer ETH, an EOA signs a transaction moving funds; to trigger a contract-managed transfer, an EOA calls the contract function which executes logic and then performs the transfer under the contract's rules. A common misconception is to think contracts can independently initiate actions; contracts only run when invoked. This distinction affects security: private keys secure EOAs, while contract correctness secures contract accounts. When designing dApps you must plan how EOAs will authorize actions and how contract code will validate and execute those authorized operations. EOA vs Contract Account means eoas are controlled by private keys and can sign transactions; contract accounts are code-controlled and execute only when invoked.. In practical terms, who signs vs what runs: accounts under the hood. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Account distinction
keyIdea.text: EOAs are controlled by private keys and can sign transactions; contract accounts are code-controlled and execute only when invoked.

content.html:
Account Type

Externally Owned Account (EOA)

Controlled by a private key; can sign transactions and initiate actions on-chain.

Control
Private key held by a user or wallet like MetaMask.
Capabilities
Sign and send transactions; pay gas; call contracts.
Account Type

Contract Account

Code stored at an address; executes when invoked by transactions or other contracts. No private key.

Control
Governed by its code; cannot sign transactions.
Capabilities
Hold ETH, update internal storage, and respond to calls with logic.
Key takeaway

Secure EOAs with good key management and secure contract code to protect contract accounts from logic bugs and exploits.

screens.title: Setting up MetaMask and connecting to a testnet (Conceptual Walkthrough)
screens.narratorSegment: Before sending real transactions you should practice on a testnet. Conceptually the steps are straightforward and each one has a security implication. First you install a wallet and create an EOA, which means generating and safely storing a seed phrase; that phrase is your only recovery mechanism so keep it offline and secret. Next, switch the wallet to a testnet like Sepolia; testnets provide non-economic tokens for development so you can deploy and iterate without spending real ETH. Then request test ETH from a faucet using your testnet address and confirm the balance displays in the wallet. When you interact with deployed contracts on a testnet you can estimate gas and adjust parameters without financial risk. A common beginner mistake is doing development on mainnet or sharing seed phrases; always validate on testnets first and treat the wallet with the same security discipline as you would on mainnet. This conceptual setup ensures that when you begin using Web3. js and signing transactions from an EOA, you have practiced signing and understood how gas and network selection affect outcomes. screens.title: How Web3.js interacts with the EVM and contracts
screens.narratorSegment: Web3. js is a library that mediates between your application and the Ethereum network. At a high level, your app constructs transactions or calls using a contract's ABI and address; Web3. js serializes the call and sends it through a provider to the network. A provider can be a remote node, an RPC endpoint, or a wallet like MetaMask which injects a provider into the browser and handles signing. When a transaction is submitted, the provider routes it to the network where nodes run the EVM to execute any contract bytecode. For read-only functions, your app can perform a call that queries state without creating a transaction and without gas. For state-changing operations, the process requires a signed transaction from an EOA, gas, and eventual confirmation in a block. A frequent misconception is to assume Web3. js itself executes contract logic; it does not — it only helps you package and transmit instructions to the chain and to the EVM. The practical design implication is that your front-end must prepare correct ABI-encoded calls and handle user signing, while minimizing on-chain work to reduce gas costs.

Architecture

Client → Provider → EVM

Web3.js creates ABI-encoded calls and relies on a provider or wallet to sign and transmit transactions to the network.

ABI & Address
Used to encode function calls that the EVM will execute on the contract.
Provider
An RPC endpoint or injected wallet that forwards signed transactions to the network.
Signing
EOAs must sign transactions; wallets manage private keys and user approvals.
Practical example

Typical call flow

  2. Web3.js estimates gas and creates a transaction object.

screens.title: Common Mistakes: Gas, Immutability, and Testing
screens.narratorSegment: Beginners often run into three recurring pitfalls: incorrect gas handling, assuming contracts can be changed after deployment, and failing to use testnets. Incorrect gas handling includes setting gas limits too low, which causes transactions to revert, or setting gas prices too low, which delays inclusion. Because gas spent before a revert is still paid, you can lose ETH to unsuccessful attempts. Immutability means once you deploy contract code it remains on-chain; if you discover a bug after deployment you cannot change the contract bytecode. That reality requires strong testing, audits, or upgrade patterns that you plan in advance. Finally, skipping testnets leads to unexpected costs and irreversible mistakes; testnets allow you to validate gas consumption and functional behavior with no real-world cost. A concrete avoidance strategy is to always estimate gas with library helpers, set conservative limits slightly above estimates, and run full tests on a testnet faucet flow. If you might need upgrades, design a migration or proxy pattern before deployment. The critical insight is that on-chain permanence and gas economics make early planning and testing non-negotiable. screens.title: Designing Gas-Efficient Contracts
screens.narratorSegment: Gas efficiency is a central design concern for smart contracts because every on-chain instruction costs Ether. To reduce gas costs, prefer compact storage layouts, minimize loops and expensive data operations, and avoid storing large data blobs on-chain when you can store references instead. Use events for off-chain indexing rather than keeping large logs in storage, because storage writes are among the most expensive operations. Another practical technique is to move complex computation off-chain and only submit the essential result to the contract for verification, when possible. A typical example is calculating complex analytics off-chain and sending summarized proofs or signatures on-chain to save gas. A misconception is that optimizing for gas always makes code less readable; while some micro-optimizations trade clarity, many patterns—like using mappings or packing variables—deliver large gas savings without harming overall maintainability. The takeaway is to evaluate which logic truly requires consensus-level enforcement and keep that on-chain; everything else belongs off-chain to maintain a cost-effective dApp. Designing Gas-Efficient Contracts means keep on-chain logic minimal, use efficient storage patterns, and move heavy computation off-chain when feasible.. Ethereum extended the idea of a blockchain into a programmable platform, allowing developers to embed logic that runs across a distributed network. In practice, that means instead of just recording transfers of value, Ethereum hosts self-executing programs called smart contracts that run deterministically on a runtime called the EVM, or Ethereum Virtual Machine. This capability turned blockchains into a substrate for decentralized applications, powering everything from decentralized finance to digital collectibles. As you begin building with Web3. js, you'll use this foundation to deploy contracts, call functions, and handle the real costs and constraints of on-chain computation. A few practical distinctions matter early: Ether is used to pay for computational work called gas; accounts come in two forms—EOAs you control with a private key, and contract accounts governed by deployed code; and the EVM ensures every node reaches the same result when code runs. Keep these ideas in mind as the conceptual scaffolding for our hands-on Web3 work. How will these pieces influence the design and cost of your dApp?

By the end of this chapter you should be able to explain why Ethereum is different from a simple ledger, describe how the EVM executes code deterministically, and define what smart contracts do in a dApp. You will also learn to explain gas as a unit of computational work and recognize how gas price and gas limit influence transaction cost and success. Practically, you'll know the difference between an externally owned account and a contract account, how wallets like MetaMask act as EOAs, and why deployed contracts lack private keys. These competencies matter because they guide how you design interactions with a contract and how you estimate cost and security. For example, choosing to do heavy computation on-chain increases gas cost and should influence how you structure your contract versus off-chain logic. Each objective lists a concrete skill and a verification milestone so you can confirm readiness before coding with Web3. js.

This second objectives slide focuses on applying the concepts in tooling and workflows. You will learn to conceptually set up MetaMask, switch to a testnet, and obtain test ETH so you can interact with contracts without financial risk. You will be expected to reason about when to estimate gas versus when to set conservative gas limits, and how gas price affects transaction confirmation priority. Another objective is to translate high-level contract behavior into Web3. js calls: constructing transactions, signing with an EOA, and submitting them for inclusion. These practical skills let you design tests and experiments before writing production code. For instance, understanding how to use a testnet faucet prevents accidental spending on mainnet. Each objective pairs with a competency milestone so you can validate that you can complete the conceptual steps required for a safe development workflow.

At a high level, Bitcoin and Ethereum both provide decentralized ledgers, but they were designed with different primary purposes. Bitcoin focuses on secure, peer-to-peer transfer of value and serves as a digital store of value. By contrast, Ethereum was created to be programmable: it runs arbitrary code in the form of smart contracts. That difference matters when you decide which platform fits an application. For example, if your project only needs secure payments, a simple ledger is sufficient; but if you require automated, enforceable logic—like an escrow that releases funds when documented conditions are met—Ethereum's programmability provides the tooling. Another important distinction is operational: Ethereum maintains an execution environment, the EVM, which processes contract bytecode deterministically across nodes; Bitcoin's script is intentionally limited and not Turing-complete. A common misconception is to assume all blockchains are interchangeable; they are not. Design decisions—immutability, gas costs, execution model—affect security, performance, and cost for developers. Consider these trade-offs early, because they influence how you architect your dApp and whether logic belongs on-chain or off-chain. What part of your application truly requires global consensus? This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

The Ethereum Virtual Machine is the environment where smart contract code runs. Think of the EVM as a sandboxed C P U that every full node runs; it takes the contract's bytecode, executes instructions, and alters the global state in a way that every node can reproduce. Deterministic execution is critical: the same inputs must always produce the same outputs across validators so that consensus on the ledger's state is possible. Developers usually write contracts in a high-level language, such as Solidity, which a compiler converts into EVM bytecode. When a contract function is called, nodes simulate the bytecode execution with the same gas accounting so that the cost and effects are consistent. A concrete example: if a contract's function deducts tokens and emits an event, the EVM applies those state changes identically on every node. A common misconception is that the EVM executes code faster because it runs everywhere; in reality, it enforces determinism and isolation, and complex on-chain computation means higher gas costs. The practical takeaway is to design contracts with predictable, efficient logic because the EVM will execute every instruction you deploy.

Smart contracts are programs deployed to the Ethereum blockchain that execute automatically when called and when predefined conditions are met. They encapsulate rules and state; once deployed, their bytecode and storage are stored on-chain and cannot be altered, which enforces immutability and transparency. An everyday example is an escrow-like contract that releases payment when a milestone is confirmed: the contract holds funds and, after receiving an interaction that satisfies the escrow condition, executes the transfer. Because contracts are immutable after deployment, testing and design matter; mistakes in logic become permanent and often costly. A common misconception is that smart contracts eliminate trust entirely; in reality, they replace certain human intermediaries with code, but trust shifts to the contract's correctness and the security of its implementation. When building dApps, you combine front-end interfaces with contract functions to create user experiences; the contract becomes the authoritative backend. The important practical insight is to keep on-chain logic lean, minimize attack surface, and plan upgradeability or migration patterns if you expect future changes. A smart contract moves through a clear lifecycle: you write high-level code, compile it to EVM bytecode, deploy that bytecode in a transaction, and then interact with the deployed contract by sending transactions or calls. First, writing in a high-level language like Solidity makes contracts readable and easier to test. Compilation translates functions and data structures into bytecode the EVM understands. Deployment is a transaction that stores this bytecode at a contract address; deployment consumes gas because it writes data to the chain. Once deployed, interacting with the contract also consumes gas for state-changing operations, while read-only calls can often be executed off-chain without gas if they don't change state. A concrete example: you write a token contract, compile it, deploy to a testnet, and then call its transfer function to move tokens; every state change will be recorded on-chain and costs gas. Common mistakes include forgetting to set a sufficient gas limit for deployment and neglecting to test migrations across networks. The practical advice is to test on a testnet, verify gas estimates before broad deployment, and keep deployable bytecode size and complexity in mind to control cost.

Gas is how Ethereum measures the computational effort required to run operations on-chain. Every opcode executed by the EVM has an associated gas cost; simple transfers use little gas, while complex contract functions use more. Two values matter for every transaction: the gas limit, which caps the maximum gas you're willing to spend, and the gas price, which is the amount of Ether you pay per unit of gas.
